title: Words That Immigrate. What Borrowed Words Carry in Their Luggage
body: At my family's Friday table you can hear four languages in one dish's description. The salad is fresh, the soup is by feel, the dessert is something we all call by a name from a country half of us have never seen. Nobody planned this vocabulary. It accumulated the way families accumulate chairs, a little from each move. Borrowed words are usually described as traffic, flowing one way or another, a trade route between languages. That picture is too clean. A borrowed word is more like an immigrant. It arrives with luggage, takes a job the locals would not do, gets its pronunciation reshaped by its new street, and within two generations its grandchildren cannot pronounce the original any better than anyone else. Take the word that entered our table for a certain kind of hug. It came from a grandmother, through a border, through a refugee camp kitchen, and it carries in it not just hug but the specific hug of someone checking that you are still in one piece. The dictionary will tell me the etymology. It will not tell me about the checking. That part rides in the word like a smell in wood. Languages borrow for two reasons, and it is worth noticing which one you are watching. Prestige borrowing happens when the lending language is fashionable or powerful. Necessity borrowing happens when a thing or a feeling genuinely has no local name. The second kind is my favorite, because it marks the exact border of what a culture had to become able to say. A language that suddenly needs a word for a laptop sleeve is telling you something. A language that grows three words for different kinds of waiting is telling you something else entirely. The strange part is how fast the immigrants naturalize. My nephew uses a word that his great-grandfather would need three sentences to explain, and he uses it with total confidence, inside an otherwise Hebrew sentence, the way you would use any local stone. He does not hear the border crossing in it. That is the whole miracle of language. The paperwork disappears. Only the word walks around free. Some words refuse to naturalize and stay forever slightly foreign, kept on a leash by their article, pronounced carefully by everyone, the permanent guests. Every language has its permanent guests and every family has words like this too, the ones said slightly louder and with a small pause before, the ones that get a chuckle when a child says them perfectly. A word can be a hundred and fifty years in the country and still be introduced at parties. I have started writing down the words at the table that belong to no single language. The list is now a page long and it reads like the family's passport stamps. There is a word for the specific gesture of offering food a third time. There is a word, borrowed twice through two different routes, that means both a tool and a person you rely on. There is an endearment whose original meaning was a unit of weight. If you want to know where a people have been, skip the history books for an evening and eavesdrop on a kitchen. The nouns will show you the trade routes. The verbs will show you the occupations. The endearments, if you are trusted enough to hear them, will show you what the journeys cost and what survived them anyway.
